'''Lisa Joy Randall''' (born June 18, 1962) is an American [[theoretical physicist]] and Frank B. Baird, Jr. Professor of Science at [[Harvard University]].<ref name="HU">{{cite web |url=https://www.physics.harvard.edu/people/facpages/randall |title=Faculty: Lisa Randall |publisher=Harvard University Department of Physics |access-date=January 1, 2014}}</ref> Her research includes the fundamental forces of nature and [[extra dimensions|dimensions]] of space.  She studies the [[Standard Model]], [[supersymmetry]], possible solutions to the [[hierarchy problem]] concerning the relative weakness of gravity, cosmology of dimensions, [[baryogenesis]], [[cosmological inflation]], and [[dark matter]].<ref name=NAS>{{cite web |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/lisa-randall-mypwv7/ |title=Lisa Randall |publisher=NAS |access-date=December 22, 2013}}</ref> She co-developed the [[Randall–Sundrum model]], first published in 1999 with [[Raman Sundrum]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Randall |first=Lisa |author2=Sundrum, Raman |date=1999 |title=Large Mass Hierarchy from a Small Extra Dimension |journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] |volume=83 |issue=17 |pages=3370–3373 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.83.3370 |bibcode=1999PhRvL..83.3370R |arxiv = hep-ph/9905221 }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Randall was born in [[Queens]], [[New York City]], [[New York State|New York]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Crace |first=John |date=June 21, 2005 |title=Lisa Randall: Warped view of the universe |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2005/jun/21/highereducation.highereducationprofile |access-date=January 12, 2023}}</ref> She graduated from [[Stuyvesant High School]] in 1980,<ref name="edgememberbio">{{cite web |url=http://edge.org/memberbio/lisa_randall |title=Lisa Randall |website=[[Edge.org]] |access-date=January 1, 2014}}</ref> where she was a classmate of fellow physicist and science popularizer [[Brian Greene]].<ref name="colmag">{{cite news |title=The String is The Thing Brian Greene Unravels the Fabric of the Universe |work=Columbia Magazine |publisher=[[Columbia University]] |url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/alumni/Magazine/Spring2006/green.html |access-date=January 1, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060924140247/http://www.columbia.edu/cu/alumni/Magazine/Spring2006/green.html |archive-date=September 24, 2006}}</ref> She won first place in the 1980 [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]] at the age of 18 and was also named a [[National Merit Scholarship Program|National Merit Scholar]]. She attended [[Harvard University]], where she took [[Math 55]],<ref name="Rosenman">{{cite news |last=Robinson |first=Evan T.R. |date=June 2, 2009 |title=Class of 1984: Lisa Randall |publisher=The Harvard Crimson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2009/6/2/class-of-1984-lisa-randall-as/ |access-date=December 9, 2018 |quote=As a college freshman, Lisa J. Randall '84 stood out for many reasons. In her first semester, she enrolled in Math 55 and Physics 55, the most difficult freshman math and physics classes offered.}}</ref> earned a BA in physics in 1983 and a PhD in theoretical particle physics in 1987 under [[Howard Georgi]].<ref name=HU />

==Work==
Randall researches [[particle physics]] and [[cosmology]] at Harvard, where she is a professor of theoretical physics. Her research concerns [[elementary particles]] and fundamental forces, and has involved the study of a wide variety of models, the most recent involving [[Randall–Sundrum model|dimensions]]. She has also worked on supersymmetry, Standard Model observables, cosmological inflation, baryogenesis, [[grand unified theories]], and [[general relativity]].

After her graduate work at Harvard, Randall held professorships at [[MIT]] and [[Princeton University]] before returning to Harvard in 2001.<ref name=CV>{{cite web |url=http://randall.physics.harvard.edu/CVpublic.html |title=Curriculum Vitae of Lisa Randall |publisher=Harvard University&nbsp;— Department of Physics |access-date=December 22, 2013 |archive-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117022524/http://randall.physics.harvard.edu/CVpublic.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>  Professor Randall was the first tenured woman in the Princeton physics department and the first tenured female theoretical physicist at Harvard. ([[Melissa Franklin]] was the first tenured woman in the Harvard physics department.)<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.physics.harvard.edu/people/facpages/franklin |title= Professor Franklin |publisher=Harvard University}}</ref><ref name=WIP>{{cite web |url=http://womeninphysics.weebly.com/notable-female-physicists.html |title=Notable Female Physicists |publisher=weebly.com |access-date=December 22, 2013}}</ref>

=== Writing and science popularization ===
Randall's books ''[[Warped Passages|Warped Passages: Unraveling the Mysteries of the Universe's Hidden Dimensions]]'' and ''[[Knocking on Heaven’s Door: How Physics and Scientific Thinking Illuminate the Universe and the Modern World]]'' have both been on ''New York Times'' 100 notable books lists.<ref name=HU />

Between the hardback and paperback release of ''Knocking on Heaven's Door'', the quest for the discovery of the [[Higgs boson]] was actually completed, a subject discussed in the book. Scientists at the [[Large Hadron Collider]] found a particle identified as the Higgs boson.<ref>{{cite web|last1=CERN|title=The Higgs Boson|url=https://home.cern/topics/higgs-boson|access-date=July 1, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Greene|first1=Brian|title=How the Higgs Boson was Found|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/how-the-higgs-boson-was-found-4723520/?page=1|website=Smithsonian Magazine|access-date=July 1, 2017}}</ref>  She said about the discovery, that even if people don't understand everything about it, "what an exciting thing it is that people are excited that there is something fundamentally new that has been discovered."<ref name="PI">{{cite web|title=Point of Inquiry podcast|url=http://www.pointofinquiry.org/lisa_randall_knocking_on_heavens_door/|website=Point of Inquiry October 8, 2012|publisher=[[Center for Inquiry]]|access-date=July 1, 2017|date=October 8, 2012}}</ref>  Randall has an e-book entitled ''Higgs Discovery: The Power of Empty Space''.  Before the Large Hadron Collider was operating, she wrote an article explaining the discoveries that were expected from using it.<ref name="TY">{{cite web|last1=Randall|first1=Lisa|title=A Tumultuous Year at the LHC|url=http://discovermagazine.com/2009/oct/12-inside-view-hiccups-at-lhc|website=Discover magazine|access-date=July 1, 2017|date=November 12, 2009}}</ref>  She was commonly asked about the misconception that the LHC could make black holes that could destroy the planet.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pappas|first1=Stephanie|title=Large Hadron Collider Won't Destroy Earth With Planet-Eating Black Hole, Court Says|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2012/10/19/large-hadron-collider-court_n_1989630.html|website=Huffington Post, October 19, 2012|access-date=July 1, 2017|date=October 21, 2012}}</ref>  She answered that it was "not even conceivable unless space and gravity are very different from what we thought."<ref name=TY/>

Randall wrote the [[libretto]] of the [[opera]] ''Hypermusic Prologue: A Projective Opera in Seven Planes'' on the invitation of the composer, [[Hèctor Parra]], who was inspired by her book ''Warped Passages''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://seedmagazine.com/content/article/opera_in_the_fifth_dimension |title=Opera in the Fifth Dimension |publisher=Seed Magazine |access-date=December 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160627230701/http://seedmagazine.com/content/article/opera_in_the_fifth_dimension |archive-date=June 27, 2016 |url-status=unfit }}</ref>

==Professional organizations==
Randall is a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (2003)<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Fellowship: Division of Particles and Fields Fellowship|url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship/dpf-fellowship|access-date=December 13, 2025|website=aps.org}}</ref> and a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2004), the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (2008),<ref name=NAS /> and the [[American Philosophical Society]] (2010).<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Lisa+Randall&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=April 21, 2021|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>

Randall has helped organize numerous conferences and has been on the editorial board of several major theoretical physics journals.<ref name=HU /><ref name=CV />

==Awards and honors==
In autumn 2004, she was the most cited theoretical physicist of the previous five years. Randall was featured in [[Seed (magazine)|''Seed'' magazine]]'s "2005 Year in Science Icons" and in ''[[Newsweek]]''{{'}}s "Who's Next in 2006" as "one of the most promising theoretical physicists of her generation". In 2007, Randall was named one of [[Time (magazine)|''Time'' magazine]]'s 100 Most Influential People ([[Time 100|''Time'' 100]]) under the section for "Scientists & Thinkers". Randall was given this honor for her work in theoretical physics.<ref>Rawe, Julie. "[[Time 100]]". [[Time (magazine)|''Time'' magazine]] May 14, 2007: 108.</ref>

Other honors:

*[[Andrew Gemant Award]], 2012<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/news/2012/theoretical-physicist-lisa-randall-wins-2012-gemant-award|title=Theoretical Physicist Lisa Randall Wins 2012 Gemant Award|date=November 22, 2013|website=www.aip.org|language=en|access-date=April 4, 2019}}</ref>
*Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]], 2008<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref>
*[[Lilienfeld Prize]], 2007<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm|title=2018 Stanley Corrsin Award Recipient|website=www.aps.org|language=en|access-date=April 4, 2019}}</ref>

Hansen|journal=Physics Today|issue=6 |article-number=1574 |language=EN|doi=10.1063/PT.4.0365 |bibcode=2011PhT..2011f1574. }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aapt.org/Programs/awards/klopsteg.cfm|title=Klopsteg Memorial Lecture|website=aapt.org|access-date=April 4, 2019}}</ref>

==Personal life==
:

Randall's sister, [[Dana Randall]], is a professor of computer science at [[Georgia Institute of Technology|Georgia Tech]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2009/6/2/class-of-1984-lisa-randall-as/ |title=Class of 1984: Lisa Randall Randall's Theory Increases Number of Dimensions in Physical Universe |publisher= [[Harvard Crimson]]|access-date=January 1, 2014}}</ref>

Randall is an avid climber.<ref name="sfgate.com">{{cite web |last1=Ganahl |first1=Jane |title=Confused by the whole shebang? She'll explain. |url=https://www.sfgate.com/entertainment/article/Confused-by-the-whole-shebang-She-ll-explain-2612369.php |website=SFGATE |access-date=June 5, 2024 |language=en |date=September 1, 2005}}</ref> A rockface along the Mill Creek near [[Dumont, Colorado|Dumont]] in [[Colorado]], is named Lisa Randall Wall after her by a local climbing society.<ref name="mountainproject.com">{{cite web |title=Rock Climbing in Lisa Randall Wall, Dumont vicinity |url=https://www.mountainproject.com/area/110632999/lisa-randall-wall |website=Mountain Project |access-date=June 5, 2024}}</ref> In a climbing accident, after falling from the cliff despite proper safety measures, she injured her heel.<ref name="theguardian.com">{{cite web |last1=Crace |first1=John |title=Lisa Randall: Warped view of the universe |url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2005/jun/21/highereducation.highereducationprofile |website=The Guardian |access-date=June 5, 2024 |date=June 21, 2005}}</ref>

=== Religious beliefs ===
When asked whether she believes in God, Randall said:
:"... I probably don't believe in God. I think it's a problem that people are considered immoral if they're [[Irreligion in the United States|not religious]]. That's just not true. This might earn me some enemies, but in some ways they may be even more moral. If you do something for a religious reason, you do it because you'll be rewarded in an afterlife or in this world. That's not quite as good as something you do for purely generous reasons."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Powell |first1=Corey S. |title=The Discovery Interview: Lisa Randall |url=http://discovermagazine.com/2006/jul/interview-randall/ |access-date=July 1, 2017 |publisher=Discover Magazine, July 29, 2006}}</ref>

=== Epstein controversy ===
Randall maintained multiple years of contact with financier and later convicted sex criminal [[Jeffrey Epstein]], beginning in 2004, and continued after his 2008 conviction.<ref name="crimson">{{Cite news |title=Harvard Professor Lisa Randall Maintained Years of Contact with Epstein, Flew on Jet |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2026/2/1/lisa-randall-epstein-ties/ |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=The Harvard Crimson|last=Blonigen|first=Megan L.|date=February 1, 2026|last2=Chiasson|first2=Hugo C.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Andersen|first=Travis|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/02/04/metro/harvard-epstein-docs-lisa-randall-emails/|title='What does fun consist of? For you?' Harvard physicist traded emails with Jeffrey Epstein for years, documents show|newspaper=Boston Globe|date=February 4, 2026|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In emails between the two contained in the [[Epstein files]] released by the Department of Justice, Randall joked with Epstein about his house arrest, which he was placed under after his conviction for soliciting sex with a minor in 2008, as well as Randall's lack of "Jew credit."<ref name="crimson" /> Randall also visited Epstein's private Caribbean island and flew on his private jet in 2014. When asked to respond to ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''<nowiki />'s request for comments, she declined.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Garisto |first=Dan |date=2026-02-06 |title=Epstein files reveal deeper ties to scientists than previously known |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00388-0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=650 |issue=8102 |pages=529–530 |doi=10.1038/d41586-026-00388-0 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
